thread.title: Amazon.com's Graviton CPU: A New War, A Lost Battle - Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN)

author: Paulo Santos
title: Amazon.com's Graviton CPU: A New War, A Lost Battle - Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN)
text:
Amazon.com ( AMZN ) just had a surprise announcement : It’s starting to offer AWS instances (EC2 A1) based on ARM CPUs. More than that, it’s starting to offer such instances based on its own-designed CPU no less. This CPU is named “Graviton.”
This is the start of a long-expected war. A war where ARM-based server CPUs start to take market share from Intel ( INTC ) as well as, potentially, Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ). However, for now, the war is mostly Intel's war to lose.
We knew this war was coming because of past efforts by Qualcomm (NASDAQ: QCOM ) and AMD which did not bear fruit. We also knew it because Apple's ( AAPL ) ARM-based custom designs were getting to such a performance level that they could successfully compete with x86 solutions (by Intel, for the most part, though that’s set to change with AMD joining the fray). Indeed, soon enough we'll see Apple's Mac line migrating to use its own ARM-based CPUs instead of x86 parts.
Yet only now did the war really start. Only now has an ARM-based cloud solution been made available by a relevant player (indeed, the most relevant player, AWS). So we are now faced with commenting on how this first battle will go.
The Battle Won’t Go Well How can I be so adamant? We have very little information on the new Amazon.com CPU. From Amazon.com, we basically know that:
It’s an ARM-based CPU, though with custom silicon as well. It will have the following pricing:
It will be easy to port script-based solutions into it, since it can run applications written for Amazon Linux, Red Hat Enterprise Linux and Ubuntu. On top of this information, TheRegister.com has obtained the CPUID on the new Graviton processor. It gives out the code 0xD08, which corresponds to the ARM A72 core.
Therein lies the reason why I say this first battle is most likely lost. Consider the following:
ARM CPUs are known for being a lot more power efficient than x86-based ones. But this is irrelevant for an AWS customer , since it gets billed for the time it uses the CPU and not how much power it consumes (though the pricing could and should reflect the costs to AWS). Server-bound ARM CPUs were requiring new designs, so as to take advantage of the power efficiency while delivering competitive performance. The A72, however, is an old mobile core. And an ARM core from the days of “losing to Apple,” too (the recent A76 core is the first which will come close to Apple). Although Amazon.com has said it included custom silicon in its solution, the whole core would likely have to be overhauled for it to be competitive. The A72 core was used, for instance, on Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 652, clocked at 1.8 Ghz. Thus, a single-core benchmark of this CPU should give us a good idea about the performance of that specific core. On Geekbench 4.2.3, using a LeEco Le2 powered by a Snapdragon 652 @ 1.8 GHz, it posts a 1,375 64-Bit single-core score. Now, Amazon.com’s price-competitive instances (above and below the A1) are things like the t3.small ($0.0208/hour) and t3.medium ($0,0416/hour). These instances run on 1 and 2 threads (1 core) of a “2.5 GHz Intel Scalable Processor.” The “2.5 GHz Intel Scalable Processor” we can find listed (2.5 GHz base) is the Intel Xeon Platinum 8180 Processor. It’s not impossible that there are other models, though not listed by Intel. This CPU can turbo to 3.80 GHz. On Geekbench 4.2.3, this CPU has a 4,689 64-Bit single-core score when running under Linux. Perhaps Amazon.com’s A72 instance can be run at 2.5 GHz as well. And perhaps we ought to adjust down Xeon’s score to the 2.5 GHz base frequency, since the score was likely obtained at the turbo frequency (3.8 GHz). Even in this scenario (and with linear adjustments), the A72 core would pull a 1,909 score, and the Xeon core would pull a 3,084 score – 61% faster. This explains the problem : The customer pays for CPU usage by the time used. Yet, instances based on x86 Xeon processors are massively faster. They accomplish a lot more work over the same time . Thus, for most processing work either the 1-thread (vs. 1 ARM core) or 2-thread x86 instances will remain a lot more competitive.
Even instances which need to be up constantly (think a web server) but are then burst-limited on the x86 instances still enjoy a dubious advantage when porting to the ARM instance, because the x86 base performance is still significantly higher than the ARM’s. And moreover, 1 x86 thread is cheaper (and likely faster) than 1 ARM core!
At the current pricing, I thus see mostly niche applications for the new ARM instances. I could be wrong. All of this will still have to be subjected to proper benchmarking to ascertain the outcome I'm predicting. Plus having 1 thread in a 2-thread CPU core under load can result in serious performance degradation, again leveling the ground.
However, for now, it would seem that using ARM cores from 4 generations ago (A72, A73, A75, A76) will be limiting the impact this development can have in terms of x86 usage. I think this is bound to change in two ways, though:
This is a first step. It’s likely that Amazon.com will iterate and come up with a much more competitive ARM server CPU in due time. This is even more so when it starts using the ARM A76 core and beyond, which will offer much higher performance levels. Amazon.com will likely reduce the price of these ARM instances significantly, thus making them more competitive. For Amazon.com, on a marginal basis (forgetting about the R&D costs that went into it), making these new CPUs has to be 1-2 orders of magnitude cheaper than buying Intel CPUs for the same purpose. These two motives can synergize. It will continue to be cheap for Amazon.com to produce (but not design) these kinds of CPUs. And the CPUs will improve a lot once Amazon.com uses more up-to-date technology.
Conclusion This particular battle, this particular ARM implementation, will likely show itself to not be competitive against present day x86 instances.
However, the war has clearly started. It won’t end anytime soon, and given what ARM and Apple are currently achieving this war will become a lot more difficult for Intel and AMD in the near future.
Amazon.com and cloud customers in general will eventually emerge winners, as processing power will become cheaper for all. Just not quite yet.
